lines: Picture one shift, one set of machines, and two plants that somehow come back with two different scores for it.
A changeover straddles the moment one shift hands off to the next, and a message that already arrived once gets resent and counted again on top of that.
Neither plant is lying. Something in how each one assembled the number is different.
Before chasing the gap, it's worth pinning down what this score is even built from.
Three separate factors multiplied together, each one answering a different question: was the line running, was it running at full speed, and did what it made actually pass.
Run a real, published example through both the long version and the shortcut version, and they land on the same answer. That agreement is the whole point, not a footnote.
Here's a detail that's easy to miss: no machine ever hands you a tidy block of twelve minutes of downtime.
What it actually hands you is a change. Running, then not running, then running again.
The block of twelve minutes gets built afterward, by pairing those changes up. It's a view on the data, not the data itself.
Worth reasoning through before the next reveal settles it.
A changeover starts a few minutes before the shift actually turns over, and keeps going a while after.
If you just hand the whole thing to whichever shift it started in, does that ever actually move a number anyone reports?
answer: It does, and here's exactly where.
The full day's total downtime doesn't budge either way you slice it.
But each shift's own number, the one someone actually reads on its own, comes out different depending on where that line gets drawn.

lines: Take that exact crossing interval and actually run it through a real splitting rule.
It doesn't come back as one lump assigned to a guess. It comes back as two separate, exact pieces, one on each side of the cutover.
Add those two pieces together and you get back the original, whole interval, with nothing lost and nothing invented.
Now the other half of the mismatch.
A message meant to arrive once gets resent, and it lands right on top of a downtime window that already happened.
Add up every recorded interval without checking for that overlap, and the total comes out inflated.
Merge the overlapping pieces into one before adding anything, and the real total comes back out.
A small ladder of codes, category down to the specific reason, lets someone roll a pile of individual stops up into one readable total.
But what about a stop so brief nobody had time to tag a reason to it?
It doesn't just get dropped. It shows up somewhere else entirely, inside the speed factor rather than the uptime one.
Follow one machine's failures and repairs across a window of time.
Every stretch of running time that sits between two observed failures counts cleanly toward how often this thing tends to break.
But the stretch right after the very last failure, running all the way to the end of the window, never gets closed by a second failure.
Count that stretch anyway, and you'd be crediting the machine with reliability nobody actually confirmed yet.
Take the identical raw minutes of a changeover plus a breakdown, and run them through two different bookkeeping choices.
Count the changeover as planned downtime, and you get one uptime percentage.
Count it as unplanned instead, and the exact same physical minutes produce a different one.
Nothing about the machine moved between those two numbers.
A score that checks out against a published example from two directions at once.
A table of intervals that's built, never stored outright.
A boundary handled properly, a duplicate caught and merged away.
Reasons rolled up, with the smallest stops still accounted for.
A reliability figure that refuses to count time nobody actually confirmed, and a bookkeeping choice that can shift the final number without touching a single machine.
A manager looks over this month's results and decides, starting tomorrow, that changeovers count as planned time instead of unplanned.
Does a single machine on that floor run any differently because of that decision?
answer: Not one. And that's exactly the point worth sitting with.
The parts get made at the same pace, by the same machines, in the same amount of time.
Only the paperwork describing all of that just changed.
